title: Video Streaming Platform
summary: Upload, process and stream video to millions of viewers.
problem: Design a platform where creators upload videos and viewers stream them on any device and connection, like YouTube.
functional: Process each video into several resolutions and formats
Search and recommend videos (at a high level)
nonFunctional: Playback should start in under 2 seconds
Storage and bandwidth cost dominate the design
Uploads must resume after a failure
constraints: 1 million uploads a day, 100 million hours watched a day
deliverables: Requirements and the assumptions you made
A capacity estimate (requests per second, storage, bandwidth)
A high-level architecture diagram (Mermaid or an uploaded image)
The API (endpoints and payloads) and the data model
How it scales, how it fails, and what you would monitor
The main trade-offs and what you chose not to build
hints: Where does the transcoding work happen, and how does it scale?
Why must most video bytes never touch your application servers?
reference:
```mermaid
flowchart LR
  Cr[Creator] -->|chunked upload| OS[(Object storage: originals)]
  OS --> Q[[Transcode jobs]]
  Q --> T[Transcoding workers] --> OS2[(Object storage: HLS/DASH renditions)]
  T --> M[(Metadata DB)]
  V[Viewer] --> API[API: metadata, manifest]
  V -->|segments| CDN[CDN]
  CDN --> OS2
  API --> M
  V -. view events .-> K[[Event stream]] --> Cnt[(View counts)]
```

- **Chunked, resumable upload** straight to object storage with pre-signed URLs; the API only records metadata.
- A transcoding **job per rendition** runs on a pool of workers fed by a queue, so a 4K upload fans out in parallel.
- Streaming uses **adaptive bitrate** (HLS/DASH): short segments and a manifest; the player switches quality with the viewer's bandwidth.
- A **CDN** serves nearly all bytes; popular videos stay at the edge, the long tail comes from origin.
- View counts are aggregated from an event stream, not updated per request.
- **Capacity (assumptions, adjust them).** 100 M hours watched a day is about 4.2 M viewers streaming at any moment on average (100 M x 3,600 s / 86,400 s); at about 3 Mbps each that is roughly 12 Tbps of egress, which is why bandwidth, served mostly by CDN, dominates cost. Storage: 1 M uploads a day at an assumed 300 MB average is about 300 TB/day of originals, and if the renditions together take about as much again, roughly 600 TB/day, about 220 PB a year. Transcoding: at an assumed 20 CPU-minutes per video that is 20 M CPU-minutes a day, about 14,000 cores busy around the clock, which favours a pool that scales with queue depth (or spot capacity).
- Search is a separate index (inverted index fed from the metadata DB) and recommendations are computed offline; both are out of scope here beyond naming them.
- Alternatives and trade-offs: transcode every rendition up front (fast start, high storage) versus only the popular ones and the long tail on demand (cheaper storage, slower first play); a newer codec such as AV1 saves bandwidth but costs far more compute and has uneven device support; building your own CDN is worth it only at very large scale.
